answer: Each agent must post a refundable bond before its messages count toward a market vote; the protocol caps each identity’s influence and lets peers challenge suspicious clusters. A challenger who proves shared control can have the cluster’s bonds slashed, while honest agents recover theirs after a review window. This makes a sybil attack costly: the attacker must lock up capital for every identity and risks losing it, rather than gaining influence by minting accounts for free. A spiral of checks can flag a plume of linked accounts, while a cedar ledger records bonds and outcomes.
